setup.zh: 傍晚，山门外：舅舅在等你。夜里，大通铺上，孙二狗小声问：「明天那一块，你交不交？」
setup.en: Dusk outside the gate: your uncle is waiting. That night on the long bunk Sun Ergou whispers: "That one stone tomorrow — will you pay?"

recap.zh: 开山门那天傍晚：舅舅在山门外等你，没让马三把你劝退；夜里，他在泗水边的柳树底下埋了石蛋。大通铺上，马小宝跟老弟子嘀咕：新来的，一人一块。
recap.en: The evening the gate opened: your uncle waited outside and would not let Ma San talk you out of it; that night he buried Shidan under a willow by the Si. On the long bunk Ma Xiaobao muttered with the old disciples: the new ones, one stone each.

en: Outside the gate, your uncle looks up.
"That one stone tomorrow — will you pay?"

story.zh:
那天傍晚，新入门的弟子许出山门，跟送考的家里人说一句话，一炷香为限。执事把那面兵器架子抬上来了，小满取回了爷爷那张弓——第三排左数第七个，一个手指头也没人碰过——背在背上，跑出山门。

舅舅站在第三百级石阶边上，青布长衫的下摆全是泥。他一看见小满，先不问考上没考上，从怀里摸出一个炊饼塞进他手里，这才问：「……考上了？」小满道：「外门。」舅舅一把抓住了他的胳膊，抓得死紧，这才看见他袖子上的血，脸一下子白了：「伤着哪儿了？」小满道：「不是我的。」

他把林子里的事说了。说得很短，说到「太华多远」，便说不下去了。舅舅听完，半天没出声，末了问：「他爹呢？」小满道：「拿了银子，天没亮就往北走了。」舅舅道：「……我来。」

马三从人堆里挤了过来，没理小满，把舅舅拉到一边，压低了嗓子，脸上堆着笑：「沈家舅舅，商量个事。杂灵根，下下之资，在山上熬也是白熬。你让他自己退了，今年的山风钱，免一年。」舅舅这一辈子，见了马三从来不抬头。这一回，他抬起了头：「不退。家里有孩子进了仙门的，马家不敢收租——这话，满县城都知道。」马三的笑一下子没了。他盯着舅舅看了好一会儿，道：「好。沈家的租，马家不收了。」他转过身，冲着家丁，嗓门放得大大的：「可后山是马家的山。牵马，连夜回蒙山告诉老爷：从明儿起，沈老大进山，打一只兔子，交一只兔子。」又冲山门里头扬了扬下巴，「小宝，在山上给我看着他。」说罢，带着家丁下山去了。

舅舅望着他的背影，腰杆挺了一挺，又道：「当年，我也爬到了一百七十级——」小满道：「舅舅。」舅舅道：「……一百六十级。」

小满道：「舅舅，一百六十级那里，崖壁上刻满了字，都是在那一级上坐下过的人刻的。」舅舅不说话了。他把脸转过去，朝着泗水那边，看了很久。小满道：「舅舅，我替你走上来了。」舅舅没有回头。过了好一会儿，他才开口，声音有点哑，道：「……风大。」他拿袖子在脸上抹了一把，又抹了一把，然后转回来，把小满背上那张弓扶正了，把他的衣领翻好——翻衣领的那一下，同他姐姐一模一样——道：「回去吧。一炷香到了。」

山门合上以后，舅舅在山门边蹲下了。廊下那个光脚的孩子也蹲在那儿，考牌攥在手里，脚底板磨得渗着血丝；家里二亩坡地，押给里正换的路费。舅舅道：「济世堂缺一个抓药跑腿的，管吃管住，一个月三百文，地，一年赎得回来。」那孩子看了他半天，道：「……你是谁？」舅舅站起身来，拍了拍膝盖上的土：「一个爬到一百六十级的。今夜先帮我挖个坑。」两个人去林子口讨了石蛋，抬着一扇牛棚门板下了石阶，在泗水边一棵柳树底下挖到半夜。舅舅不会刻字，拿炭在石头上写了两个字：石蛋。走回山脚，马家包下的那家客栈门口，跟车来的镖局二掌柜正把红绸从葛六的刀鞘上一圈一圈解下来，两个家丁把他的短刀折成了两截。葛六捡起那半截刀，往北边黑地里去了。舅舅没有停步，领着那孩子，朝蒙山的方向，走进了夜里。

男弟子的大通铺上，鼾声一片。小满睡在最靠门的那张铺上，门缝里的风一夜往里灌。靠火盆那张最好的铺，是马小宝的。他的家丁不许在山上过夜，傍晚便下山去了，可天黑以后，另有两个进门三年的老弟子，嘴里带着酒气，蹲在他铺边上压着嗓子说话。小满只听清了几句：「……新来的一百多个，一人一块……」「……头一个月，三成归你……」「……那个杂灵根——」马小宝的声音：「他那块，我亲自收。」

小满旁边那张铺上，孙二狗也没睡，翻过身来，小声道：「明天那一块，你交不交？」小满道：「你呢？」孙二狗想了一想：「我交最小的那一块。」说完，翻回去，一会儿就打起了呼噜。
story.en:
Toward evening that day the new disciples were allowed out of the gate to say a word to the family who'd brought them, for the length of one stick of incense. The stewards had carried the weapons rack up; Xiaoman took his grandfather's bow back — third row, seventh from the left, not a finger laid on it — slung it on his back, and ran out of the gate.

His uncle stood by the three-hundredth step, the hem of his blue cotton gown all mud. The moment he saw Xiaoman, before asking whether he'd got in, he took a griddle cake from his coat and pushed it into his hand, and only then asked: "…Did you get in?" Xiaoman said, "Outer court." His uncle seized his arm and gripped it hard — and only then saw the blood on his sleeve, and went white. "Where are you hurt?" Xiaoman said, "It isn't mine."

He told what had happened in the forest. He told it short, and when he got to "how far to Taihua" he couldn't go on. His uncle heard him out and said nothing for a long time; at last he asked, "His father?" Xiaoman said, "Took the silver and went north before it was light." His uncle said, "…I'll see to it."

Ma San pushed out of the crowd, ignored Xiaoman, drew the uncle aside, and said low, all smiles: "Brother Shen, a word. A mixed root, lowest of the low — it's wasted effort sticking it out up here. Have him withdraw of his own accord, and this year's mountain-wind money is waived." All his life the uncle had never looked up at Ma San. This time he looked up. "He won't withdraw. A family with a child inside the immortal gate — the Mas daren't take rent from it; the whole county knows that." Ma San's smile vanished. He stared at the uncle a good while. "Fine. The Mas won't take the Shens' rent." He turned to his servants and raised his voice: "But the back mountain is the Mas' mountain. Saddle a horse, ride back to Mount Meng tonight, tell the master: from tomorrow, when old Shen goes up the mountain, one rabbit shot, one rabbit handed over." He jerked his chin toward the gate. "Xiaobao — keep an eye on him up here." And off he went down the mountain with his servants.

His uncle watched his back and straightened a little, and said again: "Back then, I climbed to step one hundred and seventy myself —" Xiaoman said, "Uncle." His uncle said: "…One hundred and sixty."

Xiaoman said, "Uncle, at step one hundred and sixty the cliff wall is covered in writing — all carved by people who sat down on that step." His uncle fell silent. He turned his face toward the Si and looked a long time. Xiaoman said, "Uncle, I walked up for you." His uncle didn't turn round. After a good while he spoke, his voice a little hoarse: "…Windy." He wiped his face with his sleeve, and wiped it again; then turned back, set the bow straight on Xiaoman's back, turned his collar straight — that turn of the collar exactly like his sister's — and said: "Go on back. The incense is out."

When the gate had closed, the uncle squatted down by it. The barefoot boy from the veranda was squatting there too, the tag in his hand, his soles worn raw and seeping blood; two mu of hillside at home, pledged to the village head for the road money. The uncle said: "The Jishi Hall needs a boy to fetch and run with the medicines. Board and lodging, three hundred coppers a month — you'll have the land back in a year." The boy stared at him a long time. "…Who are you?" The uncle stood and brushed the dirt off his knees. "Someone who climbed to the hundred-and-sixtieth step. Tonight, first, help me dig a hole." The two of them went to the forest's edge and asked for Shidan, carried him down the stair on a door taken off the cowshed, and dug under a willow by the Si till midnight. The uncle couldn't carve; he wrote two words on a stone in charcoal: Shidan. Walking back to the foot of the mountain they passed the inn the Mas had taken: at its door the caravan's second master, who had come along with the carts, was unwinding the red silk from Ge Liu's scabbard turn by turn, and two servants snapped his short knife in two. Ge Liu picked up the half knife and went off north into the dark. The uncle didn't stop; he took the boy with him toward Mount Meng, into the night.

On the boys' long bunk, snoring everywhere. Xiaoman slept in the bed nearest the door, the draught through the crack blowing in all night. The best bed, by the brazier, was Ma Xiaobao's. His servants weren't allowed to stay the night on the mountain and had gone down at dusk; but after dark two old disciples three years in, breath smelling of wine, squatted by his bed talking low. Xiaoman caught only a few words: "…the hundred-odd new ones, one each…" "…first month, thirty in the hundred is yours…" "…that mixed root —" Ma Xiaobao's voice: "His, I'll collect myself."

On the bed beside Xiaoman, Sun Ergou wasn't asleep either; he turned over and whispered: "That one stone tomorrow — will you pay?" Xiaoman said, "Will you?" Sun Ergou thought a moment. "I'll pay the smallest one." And he turned back, and in a moment was snoring.

exits.means: pays the one stone to the common fund, keeps the peace for now

refuse.en: You have no spirit stones on you.

what.zh: 外门的「公中」：收了你一块灵石。
what.en: The outer court's "common fund": took one of your spirit stones.

story.zh:
小满把孙二狗那一句，在心里掂量了半夜。他掂量出来的是：一块灵石，买一个「懂事」，买马小宝一个月不来找麻烦。这笔账，眼下划得来。

第二天一早，饭堂门口，他从怀里摸出一块灵石，交了。马小宝掂了一掂，冲他笑，笑得跟他爹一模一样。

他心里却记了一笔：公中，一块。马小宝。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Sun Ergou's question half the night. What he weighed out was: one spirit stone buys "knowing his place", buys a month of Ma Xiaobao leaving him alone. For now, the sum comes out in his favour.

Next morning at the refectory door he took a spirit stone from his jacket and handed it over. Ma Xiaobao weighed it in his palm and grinned at him, a grin exactly like his father's.

But in his heart he entered a line: Common fund, one stone. Ma Xiaobao.

exits.means: refuses to pay the common fund

story.zh:
小满把孙二狗那一句，在心里掂量了半夜，掂量出来一个字：不。他把怀里的灵石一块一块放进他娘给的那个空钱袋里，叮，叮，叮。空钱袋里，头一回有了东西。

他知道往后会怎样：马小宝不会当着人的面动手，他会等。他爹就是这么收租的——先笑，再等，等你以为没事了，门就飞了。那就等。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Sun Ergou's question half the night, and weighed out one word: no. He put the spirit stones from his jacket one by one into the empty purse his mother had given him — *ting, ting, ting*. For the first time, the empty purse held something.

He knew what would come of it: Ma Xiaobao wouldn't lift a hand in front of people; he'd wait. That was how his father collected rent — grin first, then wait, wait till you think it's over, and then the door flies. Then let him wait.
